newsitem.title: USA: US TREASURIES HIGHER AT MIDDAY BUT BEST GAINS LOST.
newsitem.headline: US TREASURIES HIGHER AT MIDDAY BUT BEST GAINS LOST.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices were higher at midday on Wednesday but some of the best gains scored after the government issued benign July retail sales and wholesale price reports had been cut.

"We're still holding some gains that were due to two factors, primarily the normal positive response to a favorable Producer Price Index (PPI) and also, to a degree, relief that we did not see a more robust retail sales report," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America.

"The retail sales report we saw was solid and indicated that the household sector is coming back to life after the second quarter. But at the same time, it wasn't the type of vigorous growth that would lead the Federal Reserve to be deeply nervous," said Moran.

The Commerce Department reported that U.S. retail sales rose 0.6 percent in July after a revised 0.7 percent gain in June. Without auto transactions, retail sales rose 0.5 percent in July after a 0.4 percent June gain.
Meanwhile, the Labor Department said producer prices (PPI) slipped 0.1 percent in July, just as they did in June.
With food and energy items excluded, prices also fell 0.1 percent in July, after edging up 0.1 percent in June.

Near its best level of the day, around 0900 3DT/1300 GMT, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was priced at 97-12/32, up 1-8/32 from Tuesday's close and up 1-19/32 from session lows touched just before the data came out.
But, prompted by a mid-morning slide of the dollar against the mark, bonds erased the majority of that advance.
A recovery that began in late morning and continued into the early afternoon, put the benchmark bond at 96-17/32, up 12/32, to yield 6.64 percent.

"The market lost a lot of its gains when the dollar weakened," said Moran. "Also," he said, "some negative sentiment has crept into the market in the last week. Probably some of that was stirred up again by the dollar's softening."
Moran said it was important for investors to keep an eye on the dollar.
"The strong dollar has helped to keep our inflation rate in check," he said. "If we see that flattening, that will have some bearing on inflation performance in the months ahead."
The dollar fell following a Bundesbank warning of rising German inflation.

"The fall of the dollar against the mark drove a fair amount of the speculative flows," said Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston. "The minute the dollar fell through Friday's low against the mark, all the markets melted down. Bonds. Stocks. Everything."
Alexy said a shift in participation from speculative players to retail participants put a floor under the market.
"There was decent retail interest after the number and at the mid-morning lows," he said. "The technical trade driven by the currency markets created most of the volatility."

"There was good news at the open," said Josh Stiles, bond strategist at I.D.E.A. "Then when U.S. assets rallied after the data, the dollar didn't participate much -- and that was a source of concern. Then the dollar fell and made new lows and that coincided with reports of European selling in the bond market. Then hedge funds started to jump in and then when the dollar really fell off sharply, everyone saw it and started bailing out."
Three-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.17 percent. Six-month and year bill rates were down two and three basis points, respectively to 5.21 percent and 5.29 percent in afternoon trade.
Two-year notes were up 4/32 to 99-28/32, yielding 5.94 percent. Five-year notes were up 7/32 to 99-06/32, yielding 6.19 percent. Ten-year notes were up 9/32 to 98-8/32, yielding 6.36 percent.
